synopsis: This accepted preprint contributes author-reported experimental evidence for delegating candidate forecasting and experiment selection to language models supplied with prior experimental records. For pieces 01–03, its role is to inform delegation boundaries, evaluation safeguards, and cost/reproducibility requirements. It compares history conditions and simpler predictors, reports improved aggregate forecasts and selection outcomes, and exposes exceptions. The method changes supplied context while holding model weights fixed. Treat it as one underlying study, not independent corroboration or proof of unrestricted autonomous discovery.
limitations_and_counterevidence: The supplied publication date, October 8, falls within the authoritative September 16–October 15 window. Extraction does not independently verify the source. Static evaluations use single fixed splits; cross-environment tests concern autoregressive pretraining. Transfer-correlation intervals include zero for OLMo3-190M and Marin, Marin selection does not improve, and inference-selection regret favors kNN and ridge over the record-conditioned RWM. Multi-round gains concern five evaluations over pre-existing candidates; initial histories precede the selection budget. The scoring-price comparison does not incorporate acquiring the 171,862-H100-GPU-hour archive. Records were generated by the authors, release remains prospective, and commercial-API forecasts are not bitwise reproducible. No independent replication or external researcher assessment is supplied. These orientation fields do not substitute for passage citations.

passages.purpose: Reported scale, hardware expenditure, task scope, and within-environment forecasting result; supports qualified claims about the study rather than general efficiency.

locator.quote: Our evaluation draws on 2,653 experimental records from nine research environments spanning pretraining, post-training, and inference, representing 171,862 H100 GPU-hours of real experimentation. We distinguish two prediction settings: in-environment prediction (in-env) uses experimental records from the same environment to predict unseen interventions, whereas cross-environment prediction (cross-env) uses records from other environments to predict unseen interventions in a target environment. Our experiment reveals that large language models can learn from real experimental experience: across five environments in the in-env setting, research knowledge raises mean Spearman correlation on unseen interventions from 0.506 to 0.774.

passages.purpose: Information boundaries and fixed-weight method: target outcomes are withheld, near-duplicate intervention groups excluded from transfer histories, and records vary while parameters and inference settings remain fixed.

locator.quote:
In all three conditions, the model receives the target task \(\tau\) and queried intervention \(a\). Gains in source records are measured against their own tasks’ references. For the cross-environment evaluation, source histories exclude each held-out intervention and its near-duplicate group (Section [3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2)). The queried intervention’s outcome and post-execution metadata are withheld in every condition.
We vary the sources of records while holding \(\theta\) and inference settings fixed to evaluate learning and transfer from experience.

passages.purpose: Comparison design and limitation: matched backbone/settings, kNN and ridge controls, history-only tuning, and a single fixed static split.

locator.quote: We compare \(W_{0}\), which receives no experimental records (\(H=\varnothing\)), with \(W_{\mathrm{in-env}}\), which receives records from the evaluated environment. The RWM backbone and inference settings are held fixed across knowledge conditions. We include \(k\)-nearest-neighbor regression (kNN) and ridge regression, which receive the same experimental records and candidate inputs as the record-conditioned RWM. Their hyperparameters are selected using only the permitted history. Each static prediction evaluation uses a single fixed split shared by all predictors.

passages.purpose: Reported transfer-selection benefit with the Marin exception preserved; prevents treating an aggregate improvement as universal.

locator.quote: In cross-env selection, \(W_{\mathrm{cross-env}}\) reduces macro-average Regret@3 by 52.2% relative to \(W_{0}\), where each macro average weights the five target environments equally. Both Regret@3 and NDCG@3 improve in all targets except Marin (Table [5](#S3.T5)). Both feature-based baselines have higher macro-average Regret@3 than \(W_{0}\).

passages.purpose: Source's marginal scoring-cost estimate and its assumed GPU price; read alongside the archive expenditure in passage 1, not as a total-cost savings calculation.

locator.quote: Using the observed mean API cost of Claude Opus 5 (1M context, HIGH reasoning effort), scoring 16 candidates with one call each costs approximately $6.3. The median of the nine environments’ average compute costs per experiment is 42.3 H100 GPU-hours (Table [1](#S3.T1)), or approximately $127 at $3 per GPU-hour. Thus, scoring 16 candidates costs approximately 5% of one representative experiment.

passages.purpose: Table 4 counterevidence: columns within each metric are Random, W0, kNN, ridge, and the in-environment RWM. Inference Regret@3 is lower for kNN (1.62) and ridge (2.09) than for the RWM (2.53), despite its strong NDCG@3.
Transfer uncertainty and its conditioning assumptions; preserves intervals spanning zero for OLMo3-190M and Marin rather than presenting all positive point estimates as secure improvements.

locator.quote:
For each cross-environment target, we use 3,000 paired bootstrap resamples of the 69 semantic groups containing the 71 test interventions. Groups are sampled with replacement, retaining all interventions within each sampled group and using the same resample for every predictor. We recompute the Spearman difference in each resample and use its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the confidence limits. These pointwise intervals are conditional on the fixed histories, predictions, and recorded outcomes.

passages.purpose: Reported multi-round outcome gains and comparison against the zero-initial-history condition; must be paired with the constrained protocol and budget qualification in passage 9.

locator.quote: Initializing RWMs with in-environment or cross-environment records increases mean final best gain by 15.8% and 11.6%, respectively, relative to \(W_{0}\) under the same budget of 24 selections (Figure [2](#S3.F2)). Cross-environment records approach the performance of within-environment records and outperform the feature-based predictors initialized with the same source records.

passages.purpose: Multi-round protocol and boundary of the evidence: five evaluations, finite sampled candidates, shared arrivals, feedback from measured outcomes, and initial records outside the selection budget.

locator.quote:
We conduct five Autoresearch evaluations, each with eight rounds. Each evaluation samples 128 interventions from a pool of 231 unseen OLMo3-100M candidates, disjoint from the initial within-environment history. Candidate arrivals are organized by mechanism complexity, with 16 new candidates per round. Unselected candidates remain available. Within each evaluation, all methods share the candidate set and arrival schedule, and prediction ties are resolved by ascending fixed candidate ID.
E.2 Experimental feedback
We construct each evaluation’s discovery curve from its per-round forecasts, selections, and measured outcomes. Each forecast is conditioned on the initial experimental records and all records accumulated through the method’s earlier selections. The selection budget starts after the initial experimental records are available.

passages.purpose: Evidence provenance and reproducibility: author-generated records, prospective release review, supplied methodological documentation, and explicit commercial-API reproducibility limits.

locator.quote:
All experimental records were produced by the authors’ own experimental runs on public models and datasets; the study involves no human subjects and collects no personally identifiable information. Before release, we will review records, code, and prompts for licensing and security concerns and document their provenance and known limitations.
Reproducibility statement
The experimental records that all predictors consume are described in Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2), and the research environments and benchmark scoring are given in Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1). Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1) provides a condensed prediction prompt template and record-context construction. Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2) specifies the baseline inputs and hyperparameter selection, and Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3) describes the RWM-backbone and reasoning-effort comparisons. Appendix [D](#A4) reports prediction confidence intervals and specifies the fixed-budget selection metrics and aggregation protocol, and Appendix [E](#A5) details candidate sampling, arrival schedules, and metric definitions for the multi-round protocol. Language-model predictions depend on a commercial API and are not bitwise reproducible; we fix the model version, context window, and reasoning effort (Section [3.1](#S3.SS1)), and report averages over repeated evaluations where sampling is involved.
